SEIZURE OF THE SCHOONER 'AGNES G. DONOHUE.'
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I desire to call the attention of the government to a report that appears in the Halifax Morning Chronicle of the 17th inst., in reference to the schooner Agnes G. Donahue and her crew. This is a vessel that was owned in the city of Halifax and which some time in September last started on a sealing voyage down to the southern sealing grounds. While on her way down there she was captured by the government of Uruguay, one of the republics of South America. My information is that she was seized on November 11 last, and that the crew of nineteen men and the captain are still prisoners on board of the schooner, that they are not allowed to leave the vessel and that although a trial took place in the Supreme Court of that country, nothing whatever has been proven against the schooner. Still, she is in the hands of the government, the nineteen men with the officers are still prisoners oh board the schooner and nobody is allowed to communicate with them. I am not sure whether this matter has been brought to the notice of the government or not, but I am sure that it is a question that shoud receive due consideration and immediate attention. I have been informed that some,steps were being taken by the authorities to make good the damages to the owners of the vessel, but I am also informed that there is nothing in contemplation to be done for the men. Now, Mr. Speaker, I would respectfully urge that as provision is being made for the owners of the vessel who have lost the services of the schooner and the profits that they might have made out of the voyage, some consideration also should be shown to the men. The men were only working on shares. They had no fixed wages from the owners of the schooner. They were to receive so much for each skin that was caught. These nineteen men are thrown out of their employment and the loss entailed upon them by the three or four months idleness during which they are kept prisoners, and the time it will take them to return to their homes again is a very serious matter to them.

what is considered good authority that there is no law or regulation in that country in respect to sealing, and that this vessel was four miles off the shore when she was captured and furthermore that although there was a trial nothing was proved against her. Although this case as an international question may be considered small, still to those who are particularly concerned it is a very big question, and I urge upon the government that if justice is to be done to these parties it should be done quickly. Where the home government has to deal with a matter of this kind progress is usually very slow. I hope that in dealing with this case there will not be a repetition of those slow methods if justice is to be done to those who are immediately concerned. I would respectfully commend this matter to the attention of the government.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the question is a new one to the House I am sure,, but it is not new to the department. We had a complaint, I think, about a month ago about this act on the part of this southern republic, the seat of whose government is at Montevideo. We took the matter in hand at once and we entered into communication with the home government in order to secure the release of the men. After a couple of cables we were informed that the men had been discharged, but that the government at Montevideo intended to keep the captain in jail although there- was no law to keep him in jail, but from the information we gathered they were preparing the law to meet the case. We, therefore, again put ourselves in communication with the home government and presented the facts as we were informed. We have received no reply yet to the last communication we have had with the home government on the question. I understand that the British consul at Montevideo is doing his best under the circumstances. It is one of these extraordinary cases that will happen now and then in these countries. The hon. gentleman may rest assured that we are not at all losing sight of the question and we are anxious for an early settlement so that justice may be done to a Canadian.

speechtext: On all these canals the work of construction is under the charge of the superintending engineer. The superintendent as such has nothing whatever to do with that. There are no men in training for positions as superintendents of canals. There are men employed as labourers, for the opening and closing of gates and the turning of bridges, but there are no men who are in a lower position and who climb up step by step to a higher. I have no doubt that occasionally there might be a man who commenced on the canal as a labourer and who would eventually reach a much higher position ; but these are very few and far between, and the only thing that is left for the department to do is to select men with good business qualifications, with tact and judgment and some executive ability, because they have to carry on transactions on the canal in a business way with the public.

Here is another case of ' You did the same.' We have heard that until it has become stale ; and, to my mind, even when it was fresh -it was no justification for extravagance on the part of this government. When in opposition they charged the government of that time with extravagance and promised to do better. And now the minister tries to defend what he must know to be dishonest so far as this superintendent is concerned by saying that the same was done in previous years. The former superintendent was dismissed, and the cause of his dismissal was that he made these charges. Yet, to-day, the salary paid to the present officer is justified on the ground that it was paid to the previous occupant of the office. That is no justification. The only way to justify it is to show that the man is entitled to it. The minister says he will inquire into the matter. The grievance to which I wish to call my hon. friend's attention is one which we suffer from at Cote St. Paul. I endeavoured to obtain a redress of that grievance by writing to the employees of the department on the canal at Cote St. Paul. Last year I had some communication [DOT]with the minister ; but I think it is absolutely necessary to bring the matter before the House, and I would ask my hon. friend to give a strict order that the proper rem-Mr. EMMERSON.
edies be applied to that grievance. As the hon. gentleman is probably aware, on the Lachine canal at Cote St. Paul, there are a certain number of manufacturers who use the water-power from the canal. They depend upon that water-power to a very large extent in carrying on their manufacturing business. The complaint which I urged last year on their behalf and brought to the notice of my hon. friend, was that the water levels during the winter months are not properly kept up on all parts of the canal. There is a part of the canal below Cote St. Paul which, according to the complaints that have been made to me, is kept abundantly supplied with water, or at any rate receives a larger portion of water than the part at Cote St. Paul itself. This grievance only appears in the winter, because in the winter the supply of water in the canal for the purpose of manufacturing is not as regular as in the summer, because as is contended, the levels vary in the lake, and perhaps on account of the ice also. I will read to the House a letter I have received in connection with this matter, and then I will send to my hon. friend at his department a tabulated statement of the variations of the levels, which would be too long to read here. I really believe, after the efforts I have made to secure from the employees of the canal proper attention to this-matter, that it has been neglected, and that by bringing it to the notice of the department a word from the minister will probably suffice to procure the necessary degree of vigilance. These manufacturers suffer a great deal of annoyance, and some loss, which could be avoided if proper care were taken. This is the letter I have received from one of the manufacturers :
Dear Sir,-Attached is a copy of a letter written yesterday to Mr. O'Brien

Mr. O'Brien is one of the chief employees on the canal.

also returning his letter of the 11th instant, as sent you, having carefully noted his contentions.
If our trouble was caused entirely by low water in Lake St. Louis, as he contends, our demands would be unreasonable to say the least We have asked nothing unreasonable, however. What we have all along held is that the level below is kept up regardless of any and all conditions, while our supply level is continually fluctuating. The figures we give him in the letter attached show our position. On Monday the level below was 14 feet 4 inches, the level above was so low as to be entirely useless. No doubt some shortage at Lachine is a frequent occurrence at this season of the year, but we only ask a fair division of such shortage. Surely there is nothing unfair or unreasonable in our asking that the other users of the water bear their proportionate burden of existing conditions rather than have it all fall upon us as at present.
You will also observe the fact of the fluctuation in our supply level. One day it is up, the next it is down. Some days it is up in the-

morning and down again in the afternoon. Now if the whole cause was a shortage at Lachine, would there he this rapid fluctuation ? Would there not be a low level of more permanency than this ? We think so. The difficulty is simply that the man at St. Paul locks is instructed to keep the level below at some 14 feet 4 inches, and he does it regardless of whether we have an inch of head left or not.
Last year the trouble started in December, 1903, but this year we did not feel it until January. It always lasts until the canal is emptied, so that our period of difficulty is somewhat lengthier than the two months which Mr. O'Brien speaks of, being more like four months.
Now instead of complaining of this, which I think amounts to neglect and carelessness, at the beginning of the session when this trouble recurred, I wrote to the employees of the canal. I wrote particularly to Mr. O'Brien in regard to this. I do not think Mr. O'Brien is at fault, but X think there are some men in charge of the regulation of the levels who require to be informed by the department that they must more carefully attend to their duties. If the hon. minister will be kind enough to give such an order, I think that fact, with the fact that the matter has been discussed publicly, will bring some relief to these manufacturers who are certainly entitled to it. There is just one other point to which I wish to call the hon. minister's attention while I am on my feet. As the hon. gentleman is aware there is going to be. a bridge built at Atwater avenue this spring. I have no doubt that the bridge is at present ready, that all the structural pieces have been completed, and I have no doubt whatever that if the pieces were brought upon the ground, all the work along the canal done and everything ready it would not be necessary to take the water out of the canal for more than three weeks. That is not the opinion of an expert which I express, but it is an opinion which I have arrived at from what I have been told by builders and contractors. There is a question this spring of drawing off the water from the Rachine canal for six weeks and the opinion of the superintendent of the canal in Montreal is that it will l>e necessary to remove the water from the canal from March 15 until May 1, even though day and night work is resorted to.

The advanced rate. At the time this matter was under discussion in the newspapers it was first announced that a rate had been fixed by the Railway Commission by which people would have to pay a larger sum. This is less than the item of last year, by $30,000. On the La-chine canal last year we asked for $133,265; this year we are asking for $133,030. The next item is the one that covers that, salaries and contingencies in collector's offices. I may say with respect to the question that has been raised that I intimated yesterday that before I had concluded with my estimates I would be in a position to announce to the House the policy of the government with respect to the continuing of the non-collection ol tolls. That has not yet reached a point where I could make an announcement. Should it be determined to discontinue the collection of tolls on the canals, we shall of necessity dispense with the services of a large number of officials. I cannot say that they have less work in a sense. They do not collect, but their time has to be given to the work. They have to keep a correct record of everything that goes through the canals; the only difference is that the parties are not called on to pay the money. That record is furnished to the department. For two seasons.

There is quite a large town there, the town of Belleville, and a regiment

of eight companies, which has no armoury. It is the policy of the government where there are regiments of that size to provide armouries, but of course the whole of Canada cannot be provided for in one year.

Where there is a country battalion, there should be an armoury, not a large armoury, but some place where the arms can be stored and which may be used as headquarters.

That would depend on the unit of the battalion. The cost runs all the way down to $5,000.

Of course the hon. minister has nothing to do with this except to put up the armouries decided upon by the Militia Department. In cases of this kind it would certainly be a great advantage to have the other ministers interested present. The Minister of Public Works is not supposed to understand thoroughly the policy of the Militia Department with regard to armouries and cannot give the explanations which the committee requires. One easily sees that if the Militia Department is going on some fixed principle as to armouries, we are entering upon a course which involves large obligations. Itwould be interesting to know how many of these armouries we have already built and how they square with the numbers of the militia in each place. Then we should know what is the minimum of the force which could reasonably expect to have an armoury. Then we should have the number and distribution of these armouries throughout the Dominion, because if the policy be a good one it will have to be applied not only to Belleville and the smaller places but generally. Quite true it is impossible to build them all in one year ; but if we start on a common policy, we should have the basis on which such expenditure is to be made. We cannot have that information to-night because the Minister of Militia (Sir Frederick Borden) is not here. I do not want to be carping but ministers seem to think they are not interested when the estimates are going through outside of their own. I do not think that is making too harsh a criticism. It may be all very well for our ministers to dine out and enjoy social festivities, but they should be here to attend to business. It is very nice to throw off dull care and get out of the atmosphere of the House when estimates, in which you are not directly interested, are on, but that is

not treating the House properly. The Solicitor General is here, showing a very good spirit of attention to business, and so is the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, i believe. But where are all the rest and where particularly to-night is the Minister of Militia and Defence when these estimates on armouries are being put through ? He ought to be here.

The construction of this building was urged upon me by the inspectors and I am probably mainly responsible for the Department of Public Woi'ks taking it up.
What will be the total cost, and how divided?

In the neighbourhood of $25,000, made up of: contract, $15,000; heating, $2,000; wiring, $500; fittings, furniture, letter-box fronts, $3,000; sidewalk damages if necessary, $500, and contingencies to make up $25,000.
What did the site cost?
It cost $707.
This is a rather expensive building in which to store records.
There is the post office in addition, of course.
The land, no doubt, is rather high. But the building is necessary. They have a considerable staff of customs officers there. This is, no doubt, an important point.
Who is the contractor?
The contractors are .T. E. Cutler and M. Vanderburg, of Welland.
Tenders were called for, I suppose?

Yes.
Mr. FOSTER, What is the building made of ?
Brick, with a stone foundation.
What rentals were paid before?

Post office, $120 and customs house, $124.
Chatham armoury, $55,000.

This is to complete building. The work is under contract. The site belonged to the government, but, as it was low, the foundation had to be heightened, which will increase the cost of the building $4,000 or $5,000 over what such a building would cost under ordinary circumstances. The total cost will be $65,000.

I must congratulate the government upon building this armoury for it is very much needed. I will ask the minister to see to it that it is completed Mr. PATERSON.
as soon as possible. We have a very worthy regiment, who are much in need of proper quarters, the present quarters being very bad.

I would ask the Minister of Public Works upon what principle the armouries are decided upon. I find in the estimates provision for armouries in a large number of places in Ontario and other provinces. We, in. Cornwall, have been promised an armoury for some time. We are not so ambitious there as some other places are; we do not want a very extravagant building. But we have one of the finest battalions in eastern Ontario and they have no place whatever to store their arms. If the government could see their way to a reasonable expenditure, even an expenditure of $8,000 or $10,000, I think we could make it meet our requirements.
Some two years ago the then Minister of Public Works visited the town of Cornwall, looked at the different sites that were proposed, and gave every assurance that the armoury would be erected in a very short time. Since then we have heard nothing whatever about it. The town of Cornwall is the centre of three counties. Stormont, Dundas and Glengarry, and I understand from the military men that it is absolutely necessary that they should have a proper building for the storing of their arms. As I say, we are not so ambitious as Brockville, Belleville. Cobourg, London and a dozen other places in Ontario. we will be satisfied with a reasonable amount. $8,000 or $10,000 for an armoury will meet the requirements. But I feel a little sore that the town of Cornwall should be ignored completely, especially as two years ago the matter was taken into consideration by the Minister of Militia and also by the Minister of Public Works, and a definite promise, I understand, was made to the military men that we would have at least an armoury in that town.

The hon. member will understand that the initiation of such a building does liot come from the Public Works Department, but from the Militia Department. I have no doubt that if the hon. gentleman makes as strong a case with the Minister of Militia as he has made here to-night, the Minister of Militia will give him every consideration. If the Militia Department asks for an armoury at that place, the Public Works Department will endeavour to make one which will be a credit to the department. I do not, of course, know the situation there, but I have no doubt in the world that Cornwall's time will come, and I am sure the Minister of Militia will be glad to listen to any representations that may be made.

I waited on the Minister of Militia some two years ago with a deputation from the town of Cornwall, and also on the Minister of Public Works. The

Minister of Militia was not very definite in his promise, but the Minister of Public Works was very definite, and gave us very positive assurances that it would be only a short time before an armoury would be erected. Subsequently the Minister of Public Works, while passing over the Cornwall canal, visited the town and was shown the different sites that were suitable for an armoury, and he expressed a very strong opinion in favour of one of them, and gave us every assurance that the building would be erected. Now we are put off again.
It wall come.
If it will come, I am quite satisfied. Might I ask the minister when it is likely to come ?
Surely the hon. gentleman does not want me to make a definite pledge after a predecessor of mine has made a pledge which the hon. gentleman says he has not carried out.
I should think the hon. gentleman would carry out the pledges made by his predecessor.
I would like to ask whether the city of Chatham furnished a site for this armoury, or did the Crown pur-. chase it ?
It is being erected on ground which belongs to the government.
How many men are going to use it ?
One regiment.

I desire to ask the hon. gentleman if any provision will be made in the city of Brantford for a parade ground. The building there is undergoing considerable alterations. I regret I was not in when they were under discussion, but I may take advantage of this item to remind the minister that we have very little ground there indeed, in fact no ground upon which a regiment can form up. The building itself is not large enough to accommodate the whole of the regiment, so that they can form up. The men of the regiment desire to know whether or not it will be possible in the near future to provide some ground in the vicinity that will be suitable for a parade ground. The hon. gentleman visited the city a short time ago, I believe, and he will know that what I ask for is a necessary adjunct to the building. I do not desire to criticise the item with regal'd to the armoury at Brantford at all, as I think the expenditure has been a wise one. and was necessary in the interest of the regiment. The regiment is now increasing its strength, I think two more companies are being raised at the present time, and this parade ground will be a very suitable adjunct to the present alterations that are going on. If the minister can see his way to provide a little
territory there, near at hand, I think it can be procured for a reasonable price, it would be much appreciated by the regiment. I would also like to ask if it is likely that the improvements now going on will be completed in the near future. They have been under way for a considerable length of time. There is a little complaint about the dilatory way in which the contract is being carried on. I think the work is very good, but the progress is not all that could be desired. I would like to be able to give our friends an assurance that it will be pressed with all possible speed, and that this parade ground will come in the near future.

With regard to the work that is being done on the drill hall, the time for the completion of the contract expires on the 6th of October, and the department will endeavour to see that the work is completed by that time. Of course it will be impossible to have it completed before then. In x-egard to the question of procuring some extra ground in connection with the building, I think that Brantford has a right to it and it will be necessary for the government to procure a small piece of ground in addition to that which we have. From the present moment I contemplate being able to purchase that ground, provided the price is satisfactory. I think the city of Brantford has done a great deal towards the erection of this armoury in providing the site. It is a beautiful site, and I think there should be some additional ground, and I hope to provide that out of the present vote without asking the House for any further sum.
iCobourg armoury, $14,500.

On the question of armouries, I may say that I brought the attention of the Minister of Militia to the condition of the 36th Peel Battalion two or three years ago. There was a promise given at that time that the matter would be taken up and considered. We have a public building in the town of Brampton at the present time and a post office in an adjoining building. With a small expenditure, provision could be made in that same building for taking care of the arms of the 36th Peel Battalion. Some objection was raised to that proposition on the ground that the Public Works Department were unwilling to allow arms to be stored in the post office building- May I ask the minister if there is any such policy on the part of the department ?

Of course, so far as I am concerned, and the department is concerned, I can see no objections to storing the arms in the public building. I shall be glad if the hon. gentleman will let me have exact details of what he wishes to be done, and I shall be glad to discuss the matter with the Minister of Militia at the first opportunity.
Does the town of Cobourg furnish the site for the armoury, or did the Crown purchase it ?
The government bought the site.
What was the cost of the site ?
What is to be the cost of the building ?
Is that for the accommodation of more than one regiment ?

In Cobourg there is the 4th Midland field battery and the 40th Northumberland regiment.
Guelph armoury, $40,000.

Guelph is the centre of military district No. 1 and is the headquarters of a number of corps. The estimated cost of the building is $125,000. The reason that the cost is larger than that of some other buildings of a similar character is on account of the large number of guns. The battery is to be doubled up and it will have twice the number of gnus.
What has prevented the work from going on ? I see that this is a rebate.
We have just got the site. We have not made any expenditure. The plans and specifications are being prepared.
Where is the Guelph armoury to be located ?
On the fair grounds facing Huskisson Street-178 feet on Huskis-son Street, 467 feet on Farquhar Street and 885 feet on Freshfield Street.
Does the hon. gentleman know the location himself ?
I do not. I never was in Guelph but once in my life.
Is it on what is called the market square ?
I am informed by the officer of the department that It is near the market square.
Does it take up all the ground they cad the fair ground ?
I am unable to give the hon. gentleman that information.
I see the architect there and I presume he would know.
It is bounded by three streets and I presume that it will naturally take in all of the ground within these three streets.

I understand that the hon. gentleman will erect the armoury beside the parade ground where the men collect for drill. In some places the selection of the parade ground has been made at a considerable distance from the heart of the town or city and by reason of the long distance from the centre of the town regiments have not done well because you cannot get young men to attend drill when the parade ground is far from the centre of the town. I am glad to know that in the city of Guelph that difficulty does not present itself. In my own city, I know, it has been the means of the regiment being disbanded. The distance to the parade ground was so great that the men would not go. They have reorganized the regiment again, but I do not know whether they are going to make any greater success of it than they did before or not. They have made a mistake in that case which I hope will not occur again.

Wherever possible the armoury ought to be accessible to the town. But, a difficulty in regard to procuring parade grounds in close proximity to the armoury presents itself when we consider the cost of land in the centre of a city.
In the city of London you have made an improvement in your armoury by having it more centrally located.
Yes, but the old armoury was not out of the way.
Where do you have your drill ground ?
They use the park.

I am glad, to see that the hon. minister approves of having the drill hall near the parade ground. I think it is a very wise plan indeed, because if a drill hall is half a mile or so away from the parade ground it is a great inconvenience, especially to city corps, with whom most of the drill is done at night. Probably the men cannot get together before seven o'clock, and if they have to assemble at the armoury and walk half a mile to the parade ground it takes up half of the evening before they get down to drill.
1 think the question of having the drill shed at or in the vicinity of the parade ground is one that should commend itself to the hon. minister.

It is impossible to carry out both of the hon. gentleman's ideas. If you were to have both the parade ground and drill shed in the centre of the city I am afraid the cost would be such that the committee would never allow the department to commit itself to the expenditure of such a large amount of money. In London there is no drill ground attached to the armoury but there is a park two or three blocks

away from tlie armoury and the regiments march to the park and drill there. It is not expected that the department shall always provide a drill ground... It is only done where the cost is sufficiently reasonable to enable the department to do so.

On this question of the Guelph armoury the right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) made a rather extended tour in Ontario during the last election, and I noticed very many references in the daily newspapers of the time to statements made hy hon. gentlemen representing constituencies and sitting on that side of the House. For instance, the former member for West Kent made the statement that he had fulfilled all the promises he had made because he had got so many thousand dollars expended in his county. On the question of the Guelph armoury I would like to draw the hon. minister's attention to this statement by the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) as published in the 'Globe ' of October 13, 1904 :
Mr. Guthrie said he had promised on his election to have the Guelph post office renovated and enlarged.
That was the promise, and to quote again:
A third promise of his had been that ho would secure armouries for Guelph, and he was glad to say that he had secured them at last and the plans were in the city now.
I wish to draw the hon. minister's attention to the fact. Perhaps he could state how hon. members on this side of the House could reach the government. That is the way hon. gentlemen opposite representing these constituencies reach the government and I thought perhaps there was a policy by which we could reach them. It seemed to be a general topic of discussion during the right hon. gentleman's tour through the province of Ontario. Whenever he went to a town an armoury was required, and the hon. gentleman representing the county, or the candidate, would stand up and say that he would get an armoury for that town if the constituency would support the present administration. I am supposing there are no politics in the hon. gentleman's department.
This is the first time I ever heard it suggested.

I suppose the hon. gentleman will repudiate the statement of the hon. member who represents South Wellington. That hon. gentleman made three promises to his electors : First, that he would get the post office renovated, and he was very glad that he had got the government to renovate it. The third was that he would secure armouries and he was glad to state to the electors that he had secured a promise from the government to erect armouries. I call the attention of the
minister to the fact and I hope he will not allow this political warfare to creep into the administration of his department.

The hon. gentleman himself within the last ten minutes has asked the department to spend $10,000 on a building in his constituency. What is to be thought of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Blain) ? Is it that he is trying to bribe his constituents by asking what is an unnecessary expenditure? I assume that hon. gentlemen on either side have a perfect right to look after the interests of their constituencies, and to make representations to the government in regard to the interests of their own districts. I prom ised to the hon. gentleman in regard to the matter which he brought up, a very sympathetic ear, and I shall be glad indeed if I am able to carry out his wishes in the matter. All ministers and all departments, I presume, are always open to have any member of the House make such representations on behalf of their constituents as they desire to make. I am always glad to hear from members on either side of the House.

In reference to the armoury of which I was speaking a few moments ago, I find in the estimates of this year that provision is made for armouries at Belleville, Chatham, Cobourg, Guelph, Hamilton, Peterborough, St. Catharines, Stratford and Woodstock.
These are not initiatory votes for any of these works. Some of them have been there for two or three years.

Some are no doubt for the completion of buildings already started. Two or three years ago we had estimates for Brockville, St. Thomas, Barrie and a number of other towns. I wish to impress on the hon. gentleman that the most important town in eastern Ontario, a town in the centre of three very important counties, has been neglected for many years notwithstanding that the military authorities interested have come here and presented the matter to the government, I think in an absolutely fair light, and have received assurances from the government that something would be done, at any rate, in the way of erecting a building in which they could store their arms; but nothing has been done. I am glad to hear the hon. minister say that it will come in due time. I would like a little more definite promise; I would like to see it come at once.
While you live ?

While I live. It has been hanging fire a good many years and I would like to see an item in the estimates for this year. As I said before we are not extravagant in our ideas. We simply want a good and substantial building suitable to meet the requirements there. I am not in

a position to say just what the requirements are as well as the officers of the battalion, who have come here on several occasions. X might say to the hon. gentleman that the officers of the 59th Battalion are not by any means all Conservatives. Those who are at the head of the battalion are very strong supporters of this government and they feel very grieved that they can get no satisfactory answer from this government as to what they are going to do in regard to an armoury there. As I said two years ago they were directed to select a site ; they selected a site and submitted it to the government but the matter hung tire and they gat promise after promise. Immediately prior to the election of last November it was stated without any question that the armoury would be erected at once and still I see nothing in these estimates for it. I, of course, expected that there would be something for the Cornwall drill hall and I have no doubt it will be in the supplementary estimates.

The hon. gentleman will understand that it is not the custom of any government to put initiatory expenditures in the main estimates. The hon. gentleman, like every one else, will have to abide in patience until the supplementaries are out. I shall be glad to listen to any representations of any hon. gentleman in reference to the matter.
Hamilton drill hall-addition, $50,000.

The item of $50,000 for the Hamilton drill hall does not cover the total expenditure that it will be necessary to make in the city of Hamilton. I know that a new regiment, a Highland regiment, has been lately formed in Hamilton, and although they have a very fair drill hall there the number of corps using that hall so crowd it that it will be necessary to make a new provision for Hamilton. I have not been able to reach the exact amount of expenditure that will be necessary because there will be some question as to wh'ether it will be necessary to build an entirely new hall or whether a part of the old hall can be used. For that reason I am not able to give the exact expenditure, but I should say that the expenditure necessary to provide accommodation will be in the neighbourhood of $125,000 or $150,000. The matter has been carefully gone into ; we have had several plans made but I have not been able to satisfy myself as yet as to the plan to be adopted. In this case I shall have to ask the House to pass the vote without any exact estimates, for the reason that I cannot tell how much of the old building we will be able to use.
I wish to read some quotations from a paper about promises by members.
The hon. gentleman is not surely going to read any promises made by the hon. member for Hamilton ?
I am going to perhaps a higher authority.
There could be no higher authority.

When the premier was in South Wellington he assured the electors that the government had joined the government of Mexico in subsidizing a steamship line to that country which would afford a market for their manufactured goods. I have been wondering since this matter was discussed in the House whether that was correct or not. The other night when the estimates went through there was no line subsidized.

I do know, as a matter of fact, that although the bargain may not have been entirely consummated, the government are in negotiation with the Mexican government for the establishment of a line, not only on the Atlantic but on the Pacific.

If my hon. friend on your right (Mr. Paterson) will make that statement I will be glad, but he would not venture to do it when the estimates were up in the House.
Hawltesbury public building, $13,000.
How much will this cost 5
This is just for completion. The estimate for the building complete is $18,000.
What is the population of Hawkesbury ?
And the postal customs revenue ?
The postal revenue is $2,944. They'are making application for a customs office there ; it is not established yet.
What are the rentals of the present accommodation ?

$120 per annum.
Kingston military buildings-barracks, Royal Canadian Field Artillery, $20,000.

This is a revote. There has been no use made of it as yet, for the reason that it is not the intention of the Militia Department to proceed with the construction of these barracks until they are able to dispose of the land on which the old barracks are erected.
Have the aid barracks been condemned as being unsanitary ?
I do not know that they have been condemned, but there have been protests with regard to them.
Have there been any reports from medical boards as to the unsanitary condition of the buildings ?

1 think there has. I think the attention of the department has been called to their unsanitary condition.
Kingston military buildings-stable accommodation for field battery, $5,000.

This is in place of the building that was burned. This amount will nearly cover the cost.
Kingston Royal Military College-addition to drill hall, $6,000.

This is for the purpose of providing a drill hall and also a building which can be used in the winter as a skating rink for the Royal Military College. Plans and specifications were prepared, but the estimate was so large that we gave instructions to have new plans made. We hope to keep the cost within $12,000 or $15,000.
Kingston Royal Military College-servants' quarters, $8,000.
What is to be the cost of that 'building ?

If the hon. gentleman will allow the vote to pass, 1 shall be very glad to send him an estimate. As a matter of fact, I spent two hours to-day in consultation with the architect of the Militia Department, and this is one of the items on which they have not the full particulars. My recollection is that the cost will be in the neighbourhood of $15,000.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Two years ago I had the pleasure of riding up past Kingston with the Minister of the Interior, and I drew his attention to the fact that in the neighbourhood of the military properties at Kingston there are two or three martello towers, which were erected there many years ago. The masonry is all in first-class condition, but during a heavy gale two or three years ago they were unroofed, and they have been left in that dilapidated condition. I think the department ought to spend a few hundred dollars in having these old land marks preserved. The Minister of the Interior fully agreed with me when I drew his attention to them.

I am very glad the hon. gentleman has brought this matter to my attention. The committee understands that the care of the military buildings is not vested in the Public Works Department, but in the Militia Department. I have asked the deputy to take a memorandum, and I will have the attention of the militia authorities called to the hon. gentleman's suggestion.
Kingston Royal Military College-stable, $5,000.
What is to be the full cost of that ?

This is a stable for the permanent corps, and it is to include quarters for the grooms. The cost will be in the neighbourhood of $18,000. I understand that these stables are built in accordance with the regulations, which require a certain space for so many horses and so many grooms.
Is this stable being built inside or outside the grounds of the college 1 I am told that objections have been raised on account of these stables being built too near the officers' quarters.

There has been no request made to the Public Works Department for any expenditure for a site, and, therefore, I presume that it must be the intention of the Militia Department to have the stables placed on the grounds owned by the department.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
The department owns* about a thousand acres of land there.
' London military buildings-magazine, $3,000.
Where is that situated ?

The magazine has not yet been built. This vote is for the purpose of building one for the permanent corps of London. It is also intended to erect one at Winnipeg, one at Toronto and one at Montreal.
London military buildings-new stores building, $10,000.

This is aiso a vote which appears in the estimates for Toronto, Montreal, London and Winnipeg. It is for the purpose of providing a building at each of the different headquarters wherein material for the department can be stored.
What kind of stores are they ?

All kinds of camp stores. The ammunition will be kept in the magazine. These buildings are to be practically fire-proof buildings, and about 65 by 48 feet in area. Each will cost in the neighbourhood of $40,000.
Where will the London building be located ?
It will be on the line of the Canadian Pacific Railway, at the edge of the government property, near the ground where a corps is stationed.
Will the work be gone on with at an early date '!
Yes. The specifications are made for some of the buildings, and we are going to build them on the same plan.
Before this military item is passed, I would like to call the attention of the minister to the condition of the drill hall, or, to speak more accurately, the drill shed at Summerside.
When we come to the items for Prince Edward Island that will be in order.

I do not see any item for Prince Edward Island, and that is the reason I put in a plea here. The drill shed at Summerside is not fit for the accommodation of the military men. It is an old building, standing on a public square. There is no floor in it, and it is absolutely impossible to use it in winter. I took occasion several times last session to talk privately to the Minister of Militia on this matter, and he promised that it would receive some attention. I think he said he would send a man down to investigate. I do not know whether he has brought the matter to the attention of the Minister of Public Works or not. If not, I would like to take this occasion to call his attention to it, in the hope that he will put a sum in the supplementary estimates to put the building into proper condition to be used or to erect a new building. We would prefer to have $10,000 voted to erect a permanent building, for the policy of the government is to erect permanent buildings for the accommodation of the militia throughout Canada.

I have explained to the hon. gentleman that the care of these buildings is not vested in the Public Works Department but in the Militia Department. 1 have asked the deputy minister to take a memorandum.

It would be a good idea to let the items that have to do with militia buildings stand and go on with the others. It is utterly absurd to take up these items and have the minister tell us that he will take notes and get from the Minister of Militia the information required.

This is the first one in which I have taken such notes. If my hon. friend will consent, I should be very glad to leave one item on which we could have a general discussion when the Minister of Militia is here.

Leave one or two.
London post office-addition to building and improvements, $20,000.
What are these improvements?

It is intended to raise the back part of the west side of the office up to the full height of the building and to take in the balance of the ground which belongs to the department at the back end of the post office. It is Intended to enlarge the working rooms down stairs and move those working downstairs to the story above.
North Bay public building, $15,000.
The customs revenue is $29,320, and the population 2,530, the cost will be about $40,000.
What justification is there for putting up a building of that size?

The population is increasing there very rapidly and it would not be wise to put up a building only suitable to the present requirements. In a growing town such as that, the department will be justified in looking to the future.
This is at the junction of the Grand Trunk Railway and Canadian Pacific Railway?

Yes.
Oshawa public building, $21,500.
There will be another vote required to complete this.
What will that cost?

A total of $31,000, including the furniture and letter boxes, &c. The postal revenue is $8,329. the custom duties $37,458, and the population, 3,494.
Ottawa departmental buildings-steel drawers and roller shelves, &c., $25,000.
That is the usual vote for the replacing of the old wooden drawers gradually with steel drawers, so as to make the buildings as fireproof as possible.
Are tenders called for?
There are only four or five firms making them and they are all asked to tender.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Who is supplying these ?
The Eclipse Furniture Company of Ottawa, the Office Specialty Company, the Cabinet Company of Gaii-anoque and a firm in Montreal.
What is the advantage in this?
As the old wooden shelving becomes worn out we are putting In model shelving and drawers.
They are not fireproof?
No doubt, but they are very much less liable to combustion than the wooden ones.

! How much was spent on that last year ?
Mr. HYMAN, From 1st of July to 31st of December, $31,000
To whom was it paid ?
I have not the details, but it was distributed among these four firms.
Is there any difference in their prices ?

I am advised that the prices are virtually the same for similar

Ottawa public building-new coal shed, $10,000.
Where is that to be situated ?

No decision has been reached yet. We have now the coal-shed on the Canal basin, but the Department of Railways and Canals, who control that basin are continually asking the department for the removal of the building. It lias storage room of only 2.500 tons. We rent another shed which holds 3,000 tons. It is not easy to find a site for a coal-shed near at hand, and we do not want to go too far on account of the cost of haulage.
From whom does the department rent this coal-shed, and for what rental ?
What are these improvements ?

It is intended to replace the present banisters in the main lobby with granite and to renew the risers. Then there will be the dressing down and re-rubbing of the stone work of the lobby. The skylights will be repaired, a certain amount of painting done and the leaded windows in different parts of the House will be repaired.
Might I suggest to the minister, at the same time, to investigate the ventilation of this chamber and lobbies. I believe it would be wonderfully improved if proper men took it in hand.

I have heard no serious complaint. Of course, the building not being exactly modern in construction, it is somewhat difficult to ventilate it properly. Any suggestions that the hon. gentleman can give me, I shall be glad to receive.

If the hon. minister will talk the matter over with members on either side of the House, I think he will understand that the ventilation is not what it ought to be. And if he will further investigate the conduits through which, as I understand, air is brought in from the side of the hill and that are covered with moss, and I might say filth, I think he will find it necessary to make some improvements.
I understood that the air came from the top of the building and reached us as pure as possible.

I am very glad that we have not had so much ventilation as we had last session. I was almost obliged to threaten some officials of the House with dire punishment if they did not cease opening the ventilators behind us, almost destroying our health by subjecting us to draughts. I say, I am glad that has not been done, and I warn the minister that I will not submit to it and that there will be a rebellion

Order.
Mr. HENDERSON

if it is attempted ;
and the hon. gentleman who called ' order ' may as well understand that we will rule the ventilators on this side, and they can do as they like about those on that side.

I shall be glad to carry out the ideas of the hon. gentleman as far as possible. But it will be easily understood that when some gentlemen come to me and complain that the room is too warm and others a moment later complain that it is too cold, it is somewhat difficult to manage the ventilators to suit all.

No doubt we have to submit to some extra heat, but I prefer that to having the windows thrown open, perhaps without a moment's warning, letting in a draught that cannot but injure the health of those in the chamber. This used to occur at six o'clock, and, if a member remained in his place a few minutes after six, lie was subjected to a draught which would give him a severe cold in a minute or two.
I trust that the officers have learned a better way to ventilate the House, or that they will at least warn the members to retire before they open the windows.

Of course, the ventilation is more pressing during the warmer weather. And, of course, advantage is taken of the recess at six o'clock to ventilate the chamber. But the officials should at least wait a few minutes until members have left the chamber before they open the ventilators. If the hon. gentleman will call my attention to any difficulty that may arise, I shall be glad to remedy it if I can.

Does the minister think that the amount here asked for is sufficient to do the work about this building that should be done in the near future. It seems to me to have become pretty dreary along these corridors. I used to think of the House of Commons as one of the places we read about-a sort of earthly paradise. But, walking along these corridors, I find the place not at all what I expected to find it. For my part, I would like to see it brushed up to a considerable extent in the near future. This estimate appears to me to be small in comparison with other votes that are being passed. It seems to me that there is room for a good deal of improvement. While I am on my feet, I desire to say a word-I do not know that it will be strictly in order in the discussion of this item-as to the accommodation afforded to members to carry on their corespondence. The desks in this chamber are narrow, and 1 some of us have no place to write our let-

ters but at the desks. Those who have the advantage of private rooms, of course, are all right, but any oue with considerable correspondence finds it difficult to carry it on in the House. There seems to be no' quarters where quiet prevails.
I do hot know whether this is the proper place to bring it up, but while these estimates are under consideration t think perhaps the hon7 gentleman would consider a more comprehensive plan whereby a little additional room might be obtained where the members could have occasionally the use of a room for half an hour or an hour a day, where they can retire and do a little correspondence without being disturbed, as we are in the House or in the general committee room. The item he asks for is a very small one, and I think members 011 both sides of the House would join in advocating a sufficient vote to put the affairs of the House in a satisfactory condition. I understand that the legislative buildings in Toronto furnish to the members vastly better accommodation than is furnished to members in this House. If that is the case, it appears to me the minister might ask for a more liberal allowance in order to make the members a little more comfortable than they are. It strikes me as reason-ahe that when members are spending so large a portion of their lives here it is but right to make them as comfortable as circumstances will allow.

The hon. gentleman will note that this vote is for a particular purpose. There are other votes in connection with buildings, there is also a general vote in the estimates for the care and maintenance of all the Ottawa buildings. From that vote each year a considerable amount of money is taken and spent in the direction the hon. gentleman refers to, cleaning, papering, painting and so on. We have here a large pile of public buildings. Some of the corridors are not exactly in the condition I would like to see them, and it is the intention this year to- do something in that line. Numerous improvements can be made from time to time in different parts of the build! ug. So far as accommodation to members is concerned, of course if it is the will of the committee that a larger expenditure should be made for that purpose, speaking solely for myself, I have no objection at all. I think the members of this House are entitled to more comforts than they receive at present, and they should be supplied with rooms where they can do their correspondence. As time goes on that which has always been a necessity becomes more of a necessity than ever. I do not know whether we will be able to put an item in the estimates this year. We have already considerably extended the accommodation, both for private members and for committees, the last few years. We have opened up the top flat both in the Mr. COCKSHUTT.
Senate wing and in the House of Commons wing, and probably all the space in this building that is possible to get is now fully occupied. I think the time has come when there should be better accommodation for the members themselves. I intend, to discuss the matter with my colleagues, and to ascertain whether a vote can be taken to make an enlargement of the building in some other direction. This is not of course a new matter. It has been discussed in every session since I have the honour of sitting in this House. As I say, considerable improvement has been made and more room has been furnished, but we will have to consider the necessity of going .still further.

While we are on this item I woidd like to make a suggestion about lighting the approaches to this building. In an electrical city like Ottawa I think it would be both wise and easily possible to light up the walks leading to the main building a good deal better than is done at present. The electric lights and the gas lights furnished at present are in a rather crude condition.

The minister mentioned about going over the rooms from year to year. I do not know whether it is by design or- carelessness, but I certainly think that the members of the opposition are deserving of better quarters than they now receive in room No. 6.

I understand that two years ago, during recess* No. 6 was done over. Still I shall be very glad to do whatever is required there. As regards lighting, there is a vote now in the estimates for the purpose of improving the lighting. 'The matter is being attended to by the department. I will try and devise some means both of increasing the light and making a better appearance.

I am glad this subject has come up. I -was rather surprised when I came to this House to find that the members were so poorly housed. They have indeed very poor accommodation, in fact almost none at all. In Toronto the members are very much better accommodated ; no doubt the Toronto house is more modern and is provided with more conveniences. The quarters provided tor the opposition in this House are certainly very inadequate. We are shut up in a little room with only three easy chairs in it for sixty or seventy members. It does seem to me that we deserve a little better accommodation than that. Even the Speaker's quarters here are poor compared with those afforded in Toronto. It would be well worth while to consider whether the Speaker's quarters might not be moved outside of this building and thereby afford so much more accommodation for private members. We

have to pass four, six and seven months of our time in this House, and, I think, we deserve more accommodation, and some place where we can do our correspondence without being interrupted.
I understand that some measurements are being taken around this building now ; is that with a view of enlarging the building ?

I do mot think any measurements are being taken with a view of enlarging the building. Certain levels are being taken in connection with the Georgian bay canal survey. The matter has been discussed a number of times in the House, and a number of schemes have been submitted. I hope to be able to convince my colleagues that the time has come for the necessary enlargement of the quarters for members. There has been a scheme to have an extension from the present quarters occupied by the Speaker out to a line drawn from the building running north and south. That would provide a considerable number of quarters. The matter is under discussion at the present time. I do not know whether I will be able to include a vote for that this year, but I have taken the matter up and I am endeavouring to impress upon my colleagues the necessity for such an addition.

JVhile speaking of inconveniences in and around the House, 1 desire to draw attention to another matter to which I think I have never heard any reference made in this House. I refer to the character of the desks we have in this chamber. When the model for this desk was made 1 do not know. I think it must have been somewhere back about the time of Adam because it is something very ancient. 1 cannot conceive why it ever entered into the mind of the man who had charge of the furnishing of this chamber to put in desks with sloping covers. Why we cannot have a desk with a flat top on which we can place a book and know that it will not slide off and tumble on the floor is something that I cannot understand. These sloping desks are responsible for more profanity in this chamber than anything else I can conceive of. I believe that if a careful estimate were made of the books of reference from the library, the binding of which is practically destroyed from year to year by their sliding off the desks on the floor, there would be sufficient money saved in the course of a few years to put in desks properly constructed. There would not only be a saving in money but I need not tell hon. members of this House what a terrible nuisance would be avoided. An hon. member may get up to speak. He requires to have several volumes before him, probably copies of ' Hansard,' sessional reports of various kinds, or perhaps nothing more than sheets of paper. He lays them on his desk 50	,
but the first thing he knows they are at his feet on the carpet. It is a terrible nuisance but it is one of those things that can be remedied and if it does cost a little money I think it would be worth while to make the change which I suggest. I wonder that this matter has not received the attention of the Minister of Public Works before this time or whoever has charge of this building. I am quite in earnest in what I say. I am not talking for talking's sake. If this improvement can be made it will be one which will be appreciated' by every hon. member of this House. I see no advantage whatever in a desk with a sloping cover. I think we could all write on a flat topped desk just as well as we can on one that has a sloping cover. I invite the hon. minister's -attention to the matter and I feel sure that he will find some way out of the difficulty and that before long we will be provided with more modern furniture and something that will not cause hon. members to reflect in such very strong language on the neglect of the government as I am sure many hon. members are obliged to do.
ilr. McINTYRE. Mr. Chairman, there have been a good many objections taken in regard to various points in connection with the accommodation in this House, and I do not wish to add to the number, but I do wish to express my sympathy with some of the points raised. As a new member I have not felt pleased or satisfied with the amount of accommodation given in various ways in rooms for correspondence. I have particularly felt the absence of a good strong light in this House and think that if changes were made in the desks it would certainly add to the convenience of members and by making them of a light colour they might reflect the light rather than absorb it. My strongest feeling of sympathy goes out to the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) in regard to what he said on the suo-ject of draughts. The ventilation is not good and I suppose the lack of ventilation has caused those who are responsible to endeavour to supply it in some other way. During the evenings that I spent here in the earlier part of the session, I was conscious of the existence of strong draughts. I made various excursions upstairs to find out where they came from. I did not succeed in finding out but I was still conscious of the draught and of the results after leaving the House. At the present time I am conscious of a strong draught which apparently comes from this opening behind me. After I sit here I frequently have an attack of neuralgia and I sympathize very much with the hon. member for Halton if he has suffered in this way. I hope the ventilation may be improved in such a way as to do away with these draughts.

My hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson) has spoken about books falling off the desks. One reason why books



fall off the desks so much is that the index to the ' Hansard ' has been changed and it has been changed for the worse. I wish to enter my strong protest against the system of indexing the ' Hansard ' that we now have. An hon. member may have four out of the five volumes and yet he is obliged to send to the library for the fifth volume to get the complete index. I hope that the committee in charge of the debates will revert to the old style of index so that when a member takes up a volume of ' Hansard ' and looks over the index he will find what he wants.

That is as it should be.
* Mr. INGRAM. It is the worst system of indexing We have ever had in this House since I have been a member of it, and the sooner it is changed the better. Here are five volumes of the ' Hansard ' of last session. You may send for four of them and then you are obliged to send for the fifth in order to get the complete index. I do not know who advised the change but whoever did was very ill-advised.

That is a matter which is under the control of the Debates Committee, but I will see that the hon. gentleman's remarks as reported in ' Hansard ' are forwarded to the committee. As far as the question of desks is concerned, I have never heard a complaint of that kind made before. I have had several books fail from the desk but I have always found other reasons for getting rid of any profanity without taking advantage of that particular one. If any hon. gentlemen would like their desks made in the way which the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) suggests I shall be very glad to have it done. It is not necessary that they should all be changed. If my hon. friend from Halton desires his desk made in that way I will have it done right away.

That is the first promise I have ever received from the government and I shall be most happy to accept the offer. I will not then be able to say that the government never did anything for me.

Does that include the pavements on both sides of the street?
This is the roadway between the two sidewalks.
Do you propose to pave it with asphalt?

There has been no decision arrived at as to whether it will be paved with asphalt or with some other kind of pavement. I understand that some of the streets connecting with this one are paved with bitulithic and some with asphalt.
What is the present roadway?	.
Part of it is paved with old blocks which are in a very dilapidated condition and the other part is a macadam roadway.
This includes the pavement between the walks? Does the government not keep up the walk on this side of Wellington street?
I understand the owners on the other side keep up the walk but the government keep up the walk on this side.
Is it just proposed to pave the part of the street facing the government property and not beyond?
It starts with government property and ends with government property.

I would ask as a matter partly of curiosity what it costs the country to keep up the four public buildings in Ottawa ? I have heard it said that it costs $100,000 a year. I do not find fault with the amount, but I should like to know what the cost Is ?
There is a vote in the estimates for that particular item and I would be very glad to give full information when that item is reached.

I understand that not only this season but in other seasons serious accidents have occurred on the sidewalk at the gate opposite the main entrance to this building owing to the sharp decline at that point not being covered with sand or ashes.
It is supposed to be, but several times I have noticed that it was not covered with sand I have called the attention of the architects and had it attended to.
I notice that part of this item is a revote and that the item has been increased by $7,000 or $8,000. How is this work to be done ? Have you had any tenders ?

When an estimate is prepared it is not always necessary to take a vote for the full, amount of the expenditure. This was in the supplementaries last year and it is not intended to vote the whole amount this year. This $35,000 is supposed to cover the total estimated expenditure. Ottawa post office-restoration of burned building, and addition of new story, $80,000.
When did the fire take place in that building ?
January 4, 1904.
Over a year ago ?
Yes.

Simply because whoever constructed the building in the first place thought it proper to have Cleveland stone, and the same kind of stone has had to be employed in the extension of the building.
Could the building not be repaired without going to Cleveland to get stone and still retain its character 1
It is not possible to get stone to work in harmoniously with this in Canada.
We have all kinds of stone in Canada.
In all buildings now being erected in Canada provision is made for the use of Canadian stone, but the appearance of this building would have been spoiled by using a different stone.
Is this being done by day labour ?
By day labour.
What is the total cost ?
The estimated cost is

That is very much more than was stated in the first place. I suppose the extra story accounts for the increased expenditure ?
50i
How many stories will there be 1
Practically four stories and the basement, two additional stories. The old building really had no top story, as owing to the way in which the roof was made it was impossible to use the top story.
It seems to me to be an extravagant piece of business. It is such a small area. I do not understand the transaction at all, it is so slow and so expensive.

In the first place the work to be done in the cutting and laying of the stone only amounts to $64,000. A great proportion of the expenditure is for the fittings for the building. Steel and iron work will cost $29,000, a new vault will cost $9,000, roofing $5,000, an elevator $6,000, the plastering and carpenter work is estimated to cost $10,000. The building has to be painted and glazed, a new clock is necessary, and then there is the heating, furnishings and fittings for the building.
What did the building cost in the first place ?
Three hundred and some odd thousand dollars.
From time to time we have voted money renewing furniture; I would like to know what becomes of the old furniture ?
A considerable amount of renewal comes from the wearing out of furniture. In the case of this building the furniture was all destroyed by Are.

In this building, desks have been discarded which many men would be glad to get for use in their offices in the building, and no one knows what becomes of these desks. Some of these are very good and some account should be taken of them.
The deputy informs me that some four or five years ago there was a large collection of disused furniture on hand and a sale of it was held.
Did it realize much ?
I think two or three hundred dollars.

Some three or four years ago I wanted to get a table which I thought would do very well for one of the rooms ; but the table disappeared as well as some of the other furniture in the same way. If the furniture is disposed of, it is just as well that the country should get the benefit of it.
I have not heard any complaint of this kind before. The hon. gentleman knows that if my attention were called to anything of the kind, I would be glad to have it inquired into.
If the hon. gentleman would inquire a little more closely, he would find out enough to satisfy him.
If the hon. gentleman as a member of the House has any reason to make that insinuation, I think he should let me have the knowledge which he possesses.

I merely point out that it would be well for the hon. minister to make some inquiries.
Ottawa, Government Printing Bureau-to replace the present wooden root by a fireproof roof and raise the walls for one additional story on main building and two additional stories on annex, $30,000.
Will this finish the work ?
It is practically intended to finish it, but there will be a small supplementary vote required.
What is the object of doing this ?

The trouble in the Printing Bureau is that the work there has increased very greatly, and the present accommodation is not sufficient. I am simply providing this addition in response to the request of the Secretary of State, who has charge of the Printing Bureau.
Is this work done by day labour ?
No, by contract.
Does the Secretary of State say that when this improvement is made we shall get the reports of the different departments more promptly ?
We will get them more quickly.
But we will not get them promptly, as we would from an ordinary printer.
The Secretary of State has been complaining that the reason he cannot get out the reports more quickly is the lack of accommodation in the Printing Bureau.

I have been informed that the trouble is that the ministers themselves do not get the reports in the Printing Bureau early enough. The Minister of Customs used to find fault with the amount of money expended by a previous government for printing done outside the Bureau, and the country was led to believe that when these hon. gentlemen came in, the Printing Bureau would do all the work. I think I am safe in saying that several thousand dollars are paid for printing outside the Bureau. The Minister of Agriculture especially gets a large subvention for a paper -he does not own the paper, of course, but his brother has stock in it. The Minister of Customs does not look as serious as I
Mr. HYMAN
have seen him on this side of the House. He is getting old like myself, and he will have to answer.
You had better be careful, then.

I think I stand as good a chance of getting through the pearly gates as he does. I saw to-day in the editorial columns of a paper a statement of the enormous sums paid for printing outside the Bureau, and I think the attention of the minister who has control of the matter should be drawn seriously to the fact. We have a Printing Bureau, and we are paying large sums of money for its extension, and I am willing to do it ; but if we have a Printing Bureau at all, we should have one capable of doing the work, instead of paying enormous sums to Grit sheets for advertising when they are not doing the *work.

I think that the fund to which the hon. member for East Northumberland (Mr. Cochrane) refers is what was familiarly known as the reptile fund, which is being continued by the present government. Hon. gentlemen opposite made serious complaints about it prior to 1896, but I fear that this reptile fund is growing very rapidly. I hope that when the Printing Bureau is extended, this fund will be somewhat reduced. I have no doubt that the Minister of Customs is quite familiar with the fund, because I have no doubt that he often used the terms along with the hon. gentleman who formerly sat in the next seat to him, but who has been elevated to the Senate. I see the hon. gentleman smiling as if he enjoyed these reminiscences of olden times. It is certainly very pleasant to us all to know that bygone days are not forgotten.

I can only say, so far as this item is concerned, that I do not remember finding fault particularly with the printing in days gone by. It did happen occasionally that there were matters which I thought might be improved, and I intimated it in as gentle a manner and in as subdued tones as I could command ; but it was not in reference to the printing. As to the reptile press, I think I have seen that term somewhere, but I am not sure that I ever used it. I do not feel that I have much to reproach myself with in regard to the criticisms I offered in days gone by. Things were not managed then, in my judgment, as well as they are now. There is perhaps room for improvement on the part of some of us, and it would certainly be a great improvement if we could get our reports out more rapidly. I may say for the hon. Secretary of State that I know that he has made representations to his colleagues time and again as to the necessity of enlarged accommodation for the Printing Bureau. I believe he bends every

energy to the work of getting out the reports. Some of them have had to be printed in outside offices ; but this has been done on terms that have met the approval of those who are competent to judge what is fair and right in such matters.
Do you have to send them to Montreal ?
I think there is a complete supervision with reference to that matter.

Does the hon. gentleman mean to say that there was not as good a supervision over that whole matter prior to 1896 ? We have no evidence beyond the statement of the hon. gentleman, given at random, that any improvement has been made. But we know there is a much larger reptile fund than formerly, and whoever has charge of the fund had better give more attention to it and see that the money is not wasted. One or two evenings ago I was very much surprised to read the long list of moneys paid newspapers supporting the government. I did not notice any, or scarcely any. sum paid to any newspaper not supporting the government. I suppose that is why it is called the reptile fund. I can see no necessity for scattering this money all over the country, when we have a Printing Bureau at Ottawa and a large staff of men to do the work.

I might point out to the Minister of Customs that previous to 1890 the reptile press was glad to get written manuscript, but under the new order of things the manuscript must be type written. The reptile press must be getting very independent, and if they received fewer favours might be glad to take written manuscript. I have the authority of the Secretary of State for what I am saying.

It would be more satisfactory if the Minister of Customs could assure the committee that after this large amount which he asks us to vote is expended on the Printing Bureau, we will be able to have work done there as rapidly and thoroughly as in an ordinary printing office. We have the statement of the Minister of Agriculture that he has had manuscript regarding the census lying in that Bureau over a year waiting to be printed. That is certainly not business like, and I cannot understand why the government does not have things put in proper shape in that Bureau. Why does not the Minister of Customs tell the House that the government will put this Printing Bureau into proper shape, so that it may be able to turn out work as quickly and as well as it can be turned out by other offices ? If manuscript regarding the census has been lying there over a year, no doubt other manuscript has had the same fate. It is quite evident that the whole thing is not managed as it should be, and I would strongly urge that it should
be looked into more carefully, and that the minister should give us a more definite statement than he is now able to do.
