Sandwich public building, $15,000.
The population is 1,450 and the postal revenue $955. There is no customs revenue.

How much do you propose to spend ?
Mr. HYiMAN. We propose to expend there about $17,000. Sandwich is the county-town of Essex, and besides, is immediately opposite the city of Detroit. We may expend a few dollars more on the elevation of. the building than we otherwise would.
Is it the policy of the department always to purchase a site for a post office building ?
During the course" of these estimates that matter has come up quite often. Municipalities sometimes offer the government a site. Of course, where the site offered is a proper one, we accept it.
That applies to armouries as well ?
Yes.
What are the rentals now paid by the government in Sandwich.
The position of Sandwich is peculiar. It adjoins the city of Windsor and Windsor has a very considerable revenue.
Not post office revenue ?
Yes.
How much ?

Over $30,000. In addition it is an exchange office with the United States, and whilst a large part of the revenue that might in one sense be attributable to Sandwich goes to Windsor, there is a great deal of distributing work done at Sandwich for which no credit appears in the revenue.
How does that affect the question ?

The hon. gentleman asked what the revenue was. I do not know what the revenue of Sandwich is as shown by the books, but these are adjoining towns rather running into each other, with suburbs, I believe, connecting.
They generally do.

I do not know to what the point of that remark may be, but 4here are many towns whose suburbs Mr. BLAIN.
do not connect with the suburbs of other towns.
Suburbs generally connect somewhere.
I understand that there is a continuous suburb between these towns.
Sandwich is a sort of double suburb ?

The business between the two is so divided that a large part of the revenue inures to Windsor, while the incoming business, from which no revenue is derived is distributed from Sandwich, that is Sandwich has to do a great deal of work for revenue is earned but is credited to Sandwich.
Is seems a little involved.

I would be glad to make it plainer. Sometimes, it happens that people receive their letters through one post office, but send their letters out by another. In the present case there are letter-boxes along the route between Sandwich and Windsor, and as Windsor is a railway point and a point of distribution, the collectors along the route take the letters to Windsor, and the people along the route, as a rule purchase their stamps at Windsor and so Windsor is credited with a relatively large revenue.
That's not fair of Windsor, is it ?
Sandwich, at all events does not get credit for the business it does because of the circumstances I have mentioned. Nevertheless, letters are distributed through Sandwich.
Ate there two distribution ends ?
Yes, Windsor and Sandwich.
Which is the biggest end ?

I do not know what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Foster>
_ means.
The hon. gentleman (Sir William Mulock) is trying to argue that Sandwich does more business than the returns show.
I say that a part of the revenue which, under other circumstances would appear. to the credit of Sandwich goes to Windsor on account of the proximity of the two places.

It seems to me that the Postmaster General (Sir William Mulock) has made a strong argument against this grant. Letters, it appears, instead of being mailed at Sandwich are mailed at Windsor.
If the business is done at Windsor that is

the Best reason in the world why you should not have an expensive post office at Sandwich. After listening to the lucid argument of the Postmaster General I think this item should he dropped.

This is all a revote.
Why was not the work done last year ?

Some question arose as to the method in which this money should be expended. We have now arrived at a decision, the plans and specifications are ready, and we will proceed. These alterations are to be done on the main building of the custom house. In the first place, there is a change in the basement; then there is certain underpinning work, then on the ground floor a new staircase is to be built, improvements made on the front of the building, certain wooden and glass partitions have to be moved, something has to be done on the arches, laying a tile floor, the old windows to be taken out and new ones put in so as to give more light, a certain number of partitions are to be removed,
menced yet?

There are practically two works comprised under this vote, and I shall have to ask in the supplementary estimates for a considerably larger vote. Plans are all in the hands of the printers, and we shall proceed immediately with the work of raising the armoury on one side and making it deeper. In addition to that, it is necessary to provide very much more accommodation, practically the old drill hall will have to be enlarged. This is the building known as the armoury. It is contemplated to have nearly as much space in the new building as there is in the old building, it will nearly double the area, but the cost will not be as great as in the old building, because we can take advantage of one of the walls and there will not be the same amount of excavation. The building will be lengthened to the east. It is all on government ground that we own there now.

Why has this work not been done before ? The Minister of Public Works last year told us that the reason the work was not proceeded with was because of the severe weather in the winter time. Then why did not the minster proceed with that work in the summer? Now I want to know if the government are really sincere in their promise to go on now. From year to year this estimate has been put in here, and nothing has been done whatever and all the time the different corps in Toronto are cramped for want of space; indeed I think they are worse off than in any other part of Canada.

The plans for the expenditure on the armoury itself are in the hands of the printers at this moment, and that work will be proceeded with at once. As soon as the specifications are ready we will advertise for tenders, and contracts will be entered into. So far as the larger work is concerned, it will take some time to prepare the plans and specifications.
Mr. MAiCHONELL. I desire to take advantage of this occasion to call the attention of the minister to the statement his predecessor made last year in discussing this matter, on March 9. Referring to the same matter the minister said :
The plans are under consideration, and I think in a few days they will be decided upon.
' A few days ' have gone by, nearly a whole year, and nothing has been done. I can assure the minister that the people of Toronto are a good deal dissatisfied. As my hon. friend from East Toronto (Mr. Kemp) has said, the militia has not anything

like adequate accommodation for their quarters. As the minister may have heard, there has been considerable difficulty among some of the battalions, and some unfortunate unpleasantness has occurred just because of the cramped condition. The various corps endeavour to get proper accommodation, and in doing so encroach upon other regiments. Perhaps the minister is not to blame for what has occurred in the past, but I would urge upon him the wisdom and necessity of having this matter undertaken as soon as possible, and completed as soon as possible.
Toronto examining warehouse-addition to, $12,000.
That is under contract.

I would like to ask the minster if it is the intention of the government to build a new customs warehouse at Toronto, and also if it is the intention of the government to build a new post office at Toronto. I see no appropriation in the present estimates for either of those works, though possibly the minister may bring down supplementary estimates for that purpose. However, I desire to call his attention to a statement in the Toronto ' Globe ' of October 13, shortly before the then pending elections, under the heading of ' New post office for Toronto-A great building adjacent to the union station-customs warehouse, too-charges rendered necessary by railway expropriation.' Then it proceeds to say :
The application of the Grand Trunk Railway Company for an order to expropriate that part of the city of Toronto lying south of Front street, between the custom house on the east and York Street on the west, for a union passenger terminal station and other purposes, came before the Railway Commission to-day. During the discussion an important announcement was made as to what the Dominion government purposed to do in the city of Toronto. The present examining warehouse will be taken over for railway purposes, and in lieu thereof the government will build a large new examining warehouse west of the custom house on the south side of Front street. West of the examining warehouse a magnificent new general post office will be erected.
Then the article proceeds to quote Mr. Ross, superintendent of post offices. He stated :
Sir William Mulock, the Postmaster General, was desirous that such buildings would be erected as would meet the growing needs of the most important city in the Dominion from a postal standpoint. The present postal revenue of the city of Toronto is $1,000,000 per annum, and an annual expansion of from $60,000 to $100,000 had been the record during the past few years.
In the same issue of the paper appears an editorial under the heading ' The new post office and custom house':
With characteristic farsightedness Sir William Mulock has been laying his plans for perfecting the post office system of this city.

It has become the greatest revenue producing point, and more mail matter is handled here than at any other place in the Dominion.
The article commenced in that way and it concludes :
The government is to be heartily congratulated on its recognition of the needs and growth of Toronto.
This was all before the elections. We see a different aspect of affairs at the present time. In examining the estimates before the House can we see any appropriations for the purposes that were indicated in this issue of the ' Globe ' by the lion. Postmaster General ? I would like to ask the hon. minister if it is his intention to put into the supplementary estimates appropriations for these works that are spoken of in this manner in this paper ?
Does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Macdonell) desire to know what the policy of the Post Office Department is in connection with the proposed postal station near the contemplated Union statin ?
A new post office for Toronto-not a branch.

The Postmaster General has stated what his advice is. I would like to know whether the government is going to follow his advice. If that is his advice is the government going to follow his advice and are we going to have a new post office and custom house in Toronto as stated in the paper to which I have referred, the statement being made therein on his own authority ?	.

I do not know that it has been made on my own authority. I did not see the article before it was published. But, it quite represents what I would like and what I hope for. I expressed myself somewhat in that way at the Hallway Commission but our action depends somewhat on the action of the railway companies. The present Union station is west of York street and before the conflagration, not anticipating their moving their site, we had made some progress in acquiring a site for a postal station on the south-east corner of York and Front streets. That property was owned by the city but leased to the Canadian Pacific Railway and we had made arrangements with the city to convey that property to us for a figure that had been spoken of. The transfer had been practically arranged, and if it had not been for the conflagration we probably would at the present moment have been erecting our building on that land. Since then the idea has originated of abandoning the Union station at the west side of York street and building a new one easterly of York street extending to Bay street. If the railway companies carry out that policy and establish a union station coming down to Bay street then it is the policy of the Post Office Department to erect, if we can do so, if the government will agree to it and I think they will-I have no reason to doubt that they will-our postal station on the south-east corner of Bay and Front streets. If the railway companies locate the station easterly of York street then our policy is to locate our post office at the south-east corner of Bay and Front streets but we cannot conclude anything until the railway companies determine their course.
Will that new building be a general post office ?
Yes, it will do all the business of a post office but it will not mean that we abandon the one at the head of Toronto street. It will be as much a general post office as the other.
There will be no new general post office on the present site ?
Where V
At the head of Toronto street.
No.
Do I understand the hon. minister to say that the railway companies propose to take the site where the examining warehouse now is ?
I think that is part of their scheme. Is my hon. friend (Mr. Fowler) familiar with the situation of Toronto ?
Yes.

Well then he will remember that the custom house is composed of two buildings, one the custom house itself on the south-west corner of Yonge and Front streets. They do not disturb that but southerly of that and adjoining the tracks is. what we call the examining warehouse and I think they want to enlarge their strip of land so as to run their tracks through there.
Do you think it is good policy to spend $12,00b on additions to that building ?
It has all been stopped.
But I see it in the estimates.

Of course, because the contract was let long before there was any idea of touching this building at all. The very moment the department had any notification of the intention of the railway companies the work was stopped. In any case if the railways took this building they would be required to pay the government for any work that has been done on the building even if we were to go ahead and complete the building. This contract has been stopped. There is only an expenditure requisite to finish the work of some $6,000. The question is now before the department as to whether it wil not be better to spend about half of that sum, about $3,000, to complete this building temporarily so that it can be used. At the present time they can make no use of the building whatever and we are now going to make an expenditure of about $3,000. It may be two or three years before the railway companies will actually take possession of the building and in the meantime we will remain in possession. If the railway companies take over the building they will have to pay us its full value. Then, it is the intention to acquire the whole of the land between the present custom house and Bay street. The corner part of it is to be used for the erection of a postal station and another portion will be used for the erection of the examining warehouse. That is the policy of the two departments. It is necessary for the pneumatic tube service and for postal purposes generally that the post office shall be in the immediate vicinity of the station. The policy of the government depends entirely on the action of the railways.

The plans which were presented before the Railway Commission involve taking the land between the present custom house and Bay street for the Union station. Now, we are informed by the Postmaster General and the Minister of Public Works that it is the intention that this shall be taken for customs purposes and for the purpose of a sub-post office, so that the whole explanation which we have had is not at all clear. I repeat that this very site which these hon. gentlemen tell us is for the purpose of an examining warehouse, customs house and post office is the very location where it was intended to have the new union station, not west of Bay street.
They are taking more property than Bay street are they not ?
They are not going west of Bay.
They are going to York street.
There is no application.
We do not propose taking the whole depth, but the front.
I understood they intend to take the whole.
They may, but we do not.

Why, if this new building is being proceeded with, would you contemplate making this large expenditure ? These improvements were commenced after the fire, but as I understood the' minister some years would elapse before the new building is erected. May I ask the hon. gentleman when this question is to be settled?

I have no idea at all. The railways changed their plans. Their original plan was not to take this examining warehouse property from the government, but they found that it was necessary later to do so, because they could not otherwise run their tracks. No decision has yet been arrived at, and in the meantime we thought it better not to increase the examining warehouse, but to make it fit for use.

Is it not possible to hurry the matter ? The railways are slow, and the property holders' interests are being sacrificed by the long delay in dealing with the matter. Those who own the land have lost money by the delay. The government are interested ; can they not hurry the matter along ? I would press the necessity of something being done at an early date.
What ?
I do not know. I think that with the influence of the government they could do something.
Well what ?

I am not prepared to say offhand what steps could be taken, but surely something could be done by a conference between the four parties who are interested in the matter, the railways, the Railway Commission, the city of Toronto and the property holders.

I noticed a report in the papers yesterday that the Railway Commission, at a recent sitting in Toronto, determined the terms on which the valuation should be made. It is optional, I suppose, with the railway companies to buy the property or not. I do not suppose there is any way in which we can compel them to go on and complete the purchase. They have given notice and it is for them to proceed. It is very unfair for them to lock up this property. I entirely sympathize with the property holders and I think that the people who are interested in the properties there have been very badly used indeed as from the moment notice of expropriation was given, they could not go on and rebuild, yet the railway companies did not complete their purchase and then the lessees who were liable to pay rental and taxes could not rebuild, could not fix locations elsewhere for their business and the whole thing is most unsatisfactory. It is an illustration, I think, of the unsatisfactory condition of the law applicable to the expropriation of lands by railways, and I think it indicates to us that the law requires amendments so that when railways contemplate demoralizing trade by giving notice of expropriation they shall be bound by that and perhaps be considered from that moment the purchasers, subject to the determination of value. Then they could not play fast and loose. The law is very unsatisfactory but it is that way. It lias' been built up in the interests of the railways. They were here. I suppose, when we knew nothing of railway law and it is only now that we are beginning to find the weakness of our railway law. I am not making any reflections on any one or on any government ; we must all take our share of responsibility, but as I said, I think that the railway law with regard to the expropriation of lands is most unsatisfactory and unfair. There should be more mutuality about it, so that once a railway gives notice of expropriation it should be bound from that moment to proceed with the expropriation and purchase.

Are they not liable to
damages ?

I see by the newspaper reports that the commission, if they are correctly reported, found that the purchase shall be deemed to have taken place from the time of the notice, -but I believe so far as the press reports are concerned, that they did not decide whether the owners are entitled to compensation for

loss of business. That point was raised, but does not seem to have been determined.
If the railway authorities change their minds, what is the position of the property owners ?

That is a point of law ; I do not know. It would be most unfair if they had no redress. At one time there was a clause in the Railway Act saying that a railway company might desist at any time after giving notice of expropriation and arbitration, no matter what progress might have been made. They could at any moment they chose, desist and there have been cases where railway companies have abandoned proceedings after the arbitration has made some progress. Possibly getting the idea that the award was going against them they desired to have new arbitrators to start again. I think that clause of the Act has been taken out, but some years ago it was the law and it was a most unfair provision of the law.

The Postmaster General spoke of the possibility that the railway company would expropriate the examining warehouse. I would like the Postmaster General to state whether the railway company can, as a matter of law, expropriate against the government. The Minister of Public Works referred to it, but I did not think he made it definite one way **r another.

I think I was clear. There Is no question of doubt that the railway companies cannot expropriate government property, but I did not suppose that the government could stand in the way of the city of Toronto if they came to a conclusion, and if the railway companies wish to purchase that property for the purpose of an approach to the station it seems to me that we should not adopt a dog in the manger policy. We should negotiate, the railways of course paying us full value for the property. It is a matter entirely for the government to decide whether they would retain the property or not.

It will be necessary to put another vote in the supplementary estimates for the year, and if the committee will allow this vote to pass, by that time I am sure I shall have full information. The hon. gentleman is aware of the negotiations that took place for the sale of one property and the purchase of another.
Why was that done ?

Largely to meet the wishes of the city of Toronto. It was felt, from the city's standpoint, that it was better to have the barracks for the permanent force in another location somewhat further removed from the city.
When does the government have to abandon the present barracks ?
I really do not know that part of the arrangement, which was made by the Militia Department and not by the Public Works Department.
Unfortunately, the Minister of Militia is not here.
The great reason for haste is the absolute inadequacy of the present barracks.

As far as the Public Works Department is concerned, the very moment the money is available we will not lose any time in proceeding with the work.
Toronto post office-land, building, pneumatic plant and machinery, $100,000.
What has been done about that ?	4

It is intended to have a pneumatic tube system to quicken the service between the railway station and the main post offices. The department are proceeding as fast as they fairly can. The pipe has been bought by contract. It is being manufactured in Glasgow, but it will be a considerable time before it can be delivered. The tenders were for 30,000 feet in Toronto and 8,000 in Montreal at $1.45 per foot. It was bought after public tenders were called for.
Can that not be made in this country ?
No. I think the lowest Canadian tender was $5 per foot.
What is the diameter of the pipe ?
Ten inches. The city of Montreal and the city of Toronto are the only places in Canada where the department propose at present to try the system.
Where is it in existence in other parts of the world ?
In all the large cities of the United States and, I think, also in the larce cities of England.
What will be the rate of speed ?
At least a mile in two minutes.
This has nothing to do with the improvements that have recently been discussed ?

Yes ; it has to do with them so far, that we cannot determine where the terminal is to be until we know where the station is to be ; but we have ordered the pipes, and are proceeding as rapidly as we can.
Is there a vessel put in the tube ?
Yes ; a carrier.
Are there to be double tubes?
Yes.
How long does it take now to convey the mail from the post office to the depot ?

I suppose if this were to connect only with the main office, we might not adopt the system ; but Toronto is spreading out for a great distance westward. The Union station is not central, and with trains going and coming at all hours of the day, an hour's delay to a business man in getting his mail is very serious. Even the street railway is a very slow process for conveying the mails from the Union station two or three miles distant.
Instead of using your automobiles.
We have tested them and found them a failure.
They are out of commission ?
I do not know that they have all been used up but we have tested them and they have been tested elsewhere and been pronounced unworkable.
I understand that the scheme now proposed has passed the experimental stage and the minister has no doubt it will prove a success.
No doubt about it.
Are the automobiles in working order ?

I understand they are pretty well worked out excepting one machine. There were six altogether.
